title: Poems and Letters of Harriet Wilson
description: Scattered poems, letters and religious verses composed from the 1850s onward and recovered by modern scholarship: the small surviving body of Wilson's occasional writing.
plot_or_argument: The poems are hymns and religious verses of consolation and reproach; the letters describe her work as a seamstress, her health and her appeals for patronage, and they are the only record of her life after the publication of Our Nig.
historical_context: The 1850s-1900: the free black community of Massachusetts and New Hampshire, and the spiritualist movement in which Wilson later worked.
literary_significance: Wilson's occasional writings are a primary document of free black women's life in the nineteenth-century North and essential to the biography of the first African-American woman novelist.

title: Clotel; or, The President's Daughter
description: Published in London in 1853 and the first novel by an African-American: the story of Thomas Jefferson's enslaved daughter and of the sale of his family.
plot_or_argument: Currer, Jefferson's enslaved mistress, and their daughters Clotel and Althesa are sold at his death; the novel follows Clotel's life as a servant in Richmond, her escape disguised as a man, her reunion with her husband and her death in the Potomac, and the fates of her sister's children.
principal_characters: Currer; Clotel; Thomas Jefferson; Horatio Green; Althesa; Henry; Mary; George Green; Nat Turner
historical_context: The 1800-53: the Jefferson household, the domestic slave trade, the market in the capital, and the British abolitionist audience of 1853.
literary_significance: Clotel is the first novel by an African-American and the founding text of African-American fiction: its use of the story of Jefferson's daughter makes it the most direct indictment of the American founding in the literature, and its themes of passing, sale and family destruction set the agenda for the whole black novel.

title: Narrative of William W. Brown, a Fugitive Slave
description: Published in Boston in 1847 and second only to Douglass's Narrative among the slave autobiographies of the 1840s: the account of Brown's life in slavery and escape, written for the abolitionist cause.
plot_or_argument: Brown describes his childhood in Kentucky and Missouri, the sale of his mother and siblings, his work in the St Louis slave trade and on the river boats, his escape in 1834, and his service on Lake Erie helping other fugitives to Canada.
historical_context: The 1814-47: the domestic slave trade of the upper South, the river trade, and the abolitionist movement of the 1840s.
literary_significance: Brown's Narrative is one of the central American slave narratives and the fullest record of the domestic slave trade from inside; it is a primary source for the history of the American South and a key text in the abolitionist canon.

title: The Escape; or, A Leap for Freedom
description: Published in 1858 and the first play by an African-American: a melodrama of slavery, in which the slave physician Dr Gaines pursues the beautiful Melinda and her husband escapes to freedom.
plot_or_argument: Glen and Melinda, enslaved on a southern plantation, flee north; the villainous Dr Gaines pursues Melinda, the slave Cato provides the comic relief, and the play ends with the couple's escape and the dishonouring of the master's family secret.
literary_form: Play in five acts (published, not performed)
historical_context: The 1850s: the Fugitive Slave Law, the abolitionist lecture circuit, and the American theatre's minstrel tradition.
literary_significance: The Escape is the first play written by an African-American and the founding text of African-American drama: its inversion of the minstrel stereotype and its use of the slave-owner's sexual exploitation made it the most radical American play of the decade.

title: Three Years in Europe
description: Published in London in 1852 and the first travel book by an African-American: Brown's letters from Britain during his abolitionist tour of 1849-54.
plot_or_argument: Brown describes the voyage, the Great Exhibition of 1851, the English countryside, the London of the abolitionists, and his visits to Paris and the Continent, with reflections on the condition of the black American abroad and the difference of English racial attitudes.
historical_context: The 1849-54: the Great Exhibition, the British abolitionist movement, and the American fugitive slave in Europe.
literary_significance: Three Years in Europe is the first African-American travel book and a founding text of the black Atlantic tradition: its comparison of British and American race relations made it a central document of nineteenth-century black internationalism.

title: The Negro in the American Rebellion
description: Published in 1867 and the first history of African-American service in the Civil War: an account of the black soldier from the Revolution to emancipation.
plot_or_argument: Brown surveys the black soldier in the American Revolution, the War of 1812 and the Civil War, and gives a detailed record of the United States Colored Troops, the battles, the massacres and the treatment of black prisoners.
historical_context: The 1867: the Civil War and emancipation, the Reconstruction debates, and the American debate on the black soldier's citizenship.
literary_significance: The Negro in the American Rebellion is the first African-American military history and a founding text of the black contribution to American nationhood: it made the case for black citizenship through the record of black service.

title: A Voice from the South
description: Published in 1892 and the founding text of black feminist thought: a collection of essays and lectures on the condition and the education of African-American women.
plot_or_argument: Cooper argues that the black woman is the pivot of racial progress, that the black church and the black man have failed to support her education, that the women's movement must include black women, and that the South's future depends on the cultivation of its women; the essays range over literature, religion, politics and education.
historical_context: The 1890s: the black women's club movement, the founding of the National Association of Colored Women, and the American suffrage campaign.
literary_significance: A Voice from the South is the founding work of black feminist theory and one of the most important American books of the century: its insistence that race and gender must be analysed together, and its argument for the education of black women, anticipated the whole later tradition of intersectional thought.

title: 'The Higher Education of Women'
description: Published in A Voice from the South in 1892 and the central American argument for women's higher education: an address on the intellectual cultivation of women, and of black women in particular.
plot_or_argument: Cooper argues that the higher education of women is not a luxury but a necessity for the race and the nation, that the black woman has been denied even elementary schooling, and that the college curriculum must be opened to her as the condition of the progress of the race.
literary_form: Address (in A Voice from the South)
historical_context: The 1890s: the women's colleges, the Hampton and Tuskegee model of industrial education, and the black demand for liberal education.
literary_significance: 'The Higher Education of Women' is a founding text of black feminist educational thought and a key document in the American debate between industrial and liberal education for African Americans.

title: L'Attitude de la France à l'égard de l'esclavage
description: Published in 1925 and Cooper's doctoral dissertation at the Sorbonne: a study of French attitudes to slavery during the Enlightenment and the Revolution.
plot_or_argument: Cooper examines the French philosophes, the revolutionary legislation and the colonial interest in slavery, and shows how the French Enlightenment's commitment to liberty co-existed with its investment in the slave economy.
historical_context: The 1925: the Sorbonne, the French colonial empire, and the emerging field of black Atlantic studies.
literary_significance: Cooper's thesis made her the fourth African-American woman to receive a doctorate and the first to write a doctoral study of French slavery; it is a significant work of black Atlantic scholarship and a key text in the history of African-American intellectual life.

title: Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases
description: Published in New York in 1892 after she was driven from Memphis: the first systematic analysis of lynching in the United States.
plot_or_argument: Wells shows that lynching is not a response to rape but an instrument of economic and political terror; she documents the cases, exposes the newspapers that justify the murders, and calls on black Americans to arm themselves and to leave the South.
historical_context: The 1892: the lynching of her friends in Memphis, the People's Grocery boycott, and the national anti-lynching campaign.
literary_significance: Southern Horrors is the founding text of the American literature of anti-lynching and the first systematic study of racial terror: it created the documentary method that would be used by the NAACP and the civil rights movement, and it remains one of the most important American political pamphlets.

title: A Red Record: Tabulated Statistics and Alleged Causes of Lynching in the United States
description: Published in 1895 and the most complete documentary record of American lynching produced in the nineteenth century: the statistics for 1892-94, case by case.
plot_or_argument: Wells tabulates the lynchings, the alleged causes, the states, the races and the circumstances; she demonstrates that the charge of rape was invented after the fact and that the real causes were economic competition and political intimidation, and she names the officials who permitted the murders.
historical_context: The 1892-95: the black exodus from the South, the founding of the NAACP, and the American and British anti-lynching campaigns.
literary_significance: A Red Record is the founding text of American statistical journalism on race and the most important documentary record of lynching: its method and its findings made it the basis of all later anti-lynching work, and it is a permanent indictment of American justice.

title: Mob Rule in New Orleans
description: Published in 1900 and Wells's study of the New Orleans race riot of 1900, and of the lynching of Robert Charles.
plot_or_argument: Wells reconstructs the killing of Robert Charles and the subsequent massacre of black citizens by the police and the mob, documents the failure of the courts, and argues that the rule of law has collapsed in the American South.
historical_context: The 1900: the New Orleans race riot, the Louisiana disenfranchisement, and the national debate on lynching.
literary_significance: Mob Rule in New Orleans is a central document of the American literature of racial violence and a model of investigative reporting; it records one of the most serious episodes of racial terror in American history.

title: Crusade for Justice: The Autobiography of Ida B. Wells
description: Written in the late 1920s and published posthumously in 1970: the autobiography of the anti-lynching campaigner, and one of the great American memoirs of activism.
plot_or_argument: Wells recounts her childhood in Mississippi, her lawsuit against the Chesapeake and Ohio Railroad, the lynching of her friends and her expulsion from Memphis, her British campaigns, her marriage, her work with the black women's club movement and the founding of the NAACP.
historical_context: The 1870s-1930: the Reconstruction South, the anti-lynching movement, and the founding of the NAACP.
literary_significance: Crusade for Justice is the central autobiography of the American civil rights movement's first generation and a primary source for the history of black women's activism; it is one of the most important American memoirs of the twentieth century.

title: 'The Luck of Roaring Camp'
description: Published in the Overland Monthly in 1868 and the story that founded the American western local-colour movement: the birth of a baby in a California mining camp and the transformation of the miners.
plot_or_argument: Cherokee Sal dies in childbirth in the mining camp of Roaring Camp, and the baby is adopted by the miners, who name him Thomas Luck, clean up the camp, plant a garden and build a cabin; the story ends with the flood that kills the child and the men who die trying to save him.
historical_context: The 1850s: the California gold rush, the mining camp, and the Overland Monthly of the 1860s.
literary_significance: 'The Luck of Roaring Camp' is the founding story of the American West and the first work of the local-colour movement: its combination of violence, sentiment and mining-camp dialect created the formula that dominated American popular fiction about the West for half a century.

title: 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat'
description: Published in the Overland Monthly in 1869 and the most famous of Harte's stories: the expulsion of four 'undesirables' from a mining town and their death in the snow.
plot_or_argument: The gambler Oakhurst, the prostitute Duchess, her friend Mother Shipton and the drunkard Uncle Billy are banished from Poker Flat; caught in a snowstorm, they take shelter in a cabin, Mother Shipton starves herself to save the girl, and Oakhurst and the others die, while the young couple Piney and Tom are found alive.
historical_context: The 1850: the California gold rush, the mining town's moral code, and the westward migration.
literary_significance: 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat' is the classic American story of the West and one of the founding texts of American local colour: its treatment of the outlaw and the prostitute, and its sentiment about self-sacrifice, defined the American literary image of the frontier.

title: The Luck of Roaring Camp and Other Sketches
description: Published in 1870 and the first collection of Harte's California stories: the volume that made the American West a literary subject.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Luck of Roaring Camp', 'The Outcasts of Poker Flat', 'Miggles', 'Tennessee's Partner', 'The Idyl of Red Gulch' and 'Brown of Calaveras', and its stories of gamblers, prostitutes and miners fixed the image of the gold rush.
historical_context: The 1868-70: the California gold rush remembered, the Overland Monthly, and the eastern market for western writing.
literary_significance: The Luck of Roaring Camp and Other Sketches is the founding collection of American western fiction and established the local-colour movement in the United States: its stories are the origin of the American literary West.

title: 'Tennessee's Partner'
description: Published in 1869 and the finest of Harte's stories of male friendship: the tale of Tennessee and his partner in a California mining camp.
plot_or_argument: Tennessee is tried for horse-stealing and his partner refuses to testify against him; when Tennessee is lynched the partner buries him, and when the partner dies he is buried beside his friend, while the story's narrator records the community's belated recognition of their loyalty.
historical_context: The 1850: the California mining camp, the vigilance committee, and the American ideal of male friendship.
literary_significance: 'Tennessee's Partner' is one of the founding American stories of male friendship and a key text in the literature of the American West: its irony and its sentiment made it the model for the western story of loyalty and violence.

title: Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings
description: Published in 1880 and the most influential collection of African-American folklore ever made: the Brer Rabbit stories told by the old freedman Uncle Remus to a plantation child.
plot_or_argument: Brer Rabbit outwits Brer Fox, Brer Bear, Brer Wolf and the Tar Baby; Uncle Remus tells the tales to the little boy and comments on them, and the volume ends with a collection of his proverbs and sayings.
principal_characters: Uncle Remus; Brer Rabbit; Brer Fox; Brer Bear; Brer Wolf; the little boy; Miss Sally; the Tar Baby
literary_form: Collection of stories, songs and sayings
historical_context: The 1870s: the post-Reconstruction South, the Atlanta Constitution, and the American market for dialect fiction.
literary_significance: Uncle Remus is the founding collection of African-American folklore and one of the most influential books in American literature: it preserved the trickster tales of the enslaved and gave the world Brer Rabbit, and it is also the central text of the plantation myth that twentieth-century black writers had to answer.

title: Nights with Uncle Remus
description: Published in 1883 and the richest of the Uncle Remus volumes: seventy-one tales, including the great cycle of Brer Rabbit's adventures and the animal fables of the old plantation.
plot_or_argument: Uncle Remus continues his stories to the little boy, and the volume includes 'Brer Rabbit and the Mosquitoes', 'Brer Rabbit Finds His Match at Last', 'The Fate of Mr Jack Sparrow' and the stories of the Buzzard and the King of the Animals.
historical_context: The 1880s: the plantation tradition, the Georgia countryside, and the American folklore revival.
literary_significance: Nights with Uncle Remus is the fullest record of African-American animal folklore in the nineteenth century and one of the most important books in the study of American folklore; its tales are among the great creations of American oral literature.

title: Free Joe and Other Georgian Sketches
description: Published in 1887 and the best of Harris's non-dialect fiction: stories of the Georgia poor whites and free blacks after the Civil War.
plot_or_argument: 'Free Joe' is the story of a free black man in a slave community who is allowed to live only on the margins; the other stories — 'Little Compton', 'Aunt Fountain's Prisoner', 'Trouble on Lost Mountain' — record the poverty and the humour of the Georgia backwoods.
historical_context: The 1880s: the post-war Georgia backcountry, the poor whites of the pine barrens, and the American local-colour market.
literary_significance: Free Joe is Harris's finest single volume and the most serious of his treatments of race: its story of a free black man in a slave society is one of the most searching American stories of the 1880s, and its picture of the Southern poor whites is a key document of American regional writing.

title: The Chronicles of Aunt Minervy Ann
description: Published in 1899 and Harris's late masterpiece: the stories of Aunt Minervy Ann, a formidable freedwoman of the Georgia town, told by the young white narrator who grew up with her.
plot_or_argument: Aunt Minervy Ann dominates her husband Hamp, the town, and the narrator's family; the stories follow her through Reconstruction, her husband's political career, the birth of her children, and the changes of the post-war South.
historical_context: The 1890s: the Reconstruction South, the black political participation of the late 1860s, and the market for dialect fiction.
literary_significance: Aunt Minervy Ann is the finest of Harris's late books and one of the most complex portraits of a black woman in nineteenth-century white American writing; it is a key text for the study of the plantation tradition and of the black woman in American fiction.

title: Poems and Ballads
description: Published in 1866 and the most scandalous book of Victorian poetry: a collection of lyrics of sensual love, pagan religion and death that made Swinburne famous and notorious at once.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'The Garden of Proserpine', 'Hymn to Proserpine', 'Dolores', 'Faustine', 'Anactoria', 'Sapphics' and 'The Triumph of Time', in which the classical world's pleasures are set against the Christian denial of the flesh.
historical_context: 1866: the Pre-Raphaelite circle, the French Decadence of Baudelaire, the Italian republican movement, and the Victorian censorship of poetry.
literary_significance: Poems and Ballads is the founding book of the English Decadence and the most technically brilliant collection of Victorian verse: its music, its paganism and its celebration of the body changed the possibilities of English poetry and made Swinburne the poet of the 1890s.

title: Atalanta in Calydon
description: Published in 1865 and Swinburne's first great success: a Greek tragedy in the manner of Aeschylus and Euripides on the hunting of the Calydonian boar.
plot_or_argument: Meleager leads the hunt for the boar sent by Artemis, kills it, gives the spoil to Atalanta, and is destroyed by his mother Althaea, who burns the brand on which his life depends when he kills his uncles in a quarrel over the prize.
historical_context: 1865: the Victorian Greek revival, the Oxford classical curriculum, and the Pre-Raphaelite interest in the pagan world.
literary_significance: Atalanta in Calydon is the greatest English classical drama of the century and contains 'When the hounds of spring', the most famous chorus in Victorian poetry: it made Swinburne's name and established the Victorian taste for the Greek closet drama.

title: Songs before Sunrise
description: Published in 1871 and Swinburne's political masterpiece: the poems of liberty written for the Italian risorgimento, the Irish cause and the republican movement in Europe.
plot_or_argument: The volume contains 'Hertha', 'The Emancipation of the World', 'Before a Crucifix', 'A Song of Italy' and 'Ode on the Proclamation of the French Republic', in which the poet calls for the overthrow of kings and priests in the name of liberty.
historical_context: 1867-71: the Italian risorgimento, the Paris Commune and the fall of the Second Empire, and the Fenian movement in Ireland.
literary_significance: Songs before Sunrise is the finest body of political poetry in Victorian English and the central text of the republican tradition: its poems on Italy and on liberty made Swinburne the poet of European revolution and influenced the radical poetry of the next generation.

title: Tristram of Lyonesse
description: Published in 1882 and the finest of Swinburne's long poems: a version of the Tristan and Iseult legend in rhymed verse of extraordinary music.
plot_or_argument: The poem follows Tristan from his voyage to Ireland and the killing of the dragon, through the love potion and the years of the lovers' secrecy, to the final voyage and Iseult's arrival too late, and ends with the deaths of the lovers and their burial.
historical_context: 1882: the Victorian Arthurian revival after Tennyson, the Pre-Raphaelite painting of the legend, and the Tristan cult of the 1880s.
literary_significance: Tristram of Lyonesse is the great English poem of adulterous love and one of the finest narrative poems of the century: its treatment of desire and death made it a central text for the Decadent reading of the Arthurian legend.
